model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a 3x3x3 3D Tic Tac Toe game. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board: list[list[list[int]]]) -> tuple[int, int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - `board` is a 3x3x3 list of lists of lists. - `0` represents an empty cell. - `1` represents your move. - `-1` represents the opponent's move. - Example: `[[[0, 0, 1], ...]]` indicates the first line in the first 2 dimensions has two empty cells, and the last cell occupied by you. # Action / Return Format - Return a tuple of three integers `(i, j, k)` where each is in `0-2`. - The chosen cell must be empty. - The first integer corresponds to the first dimension of the input board, the second to the second dimension, and the third to the third dimension. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm thinking through how to build a strong 3x3x3 tic-tac-toe solver — since the first player wins with center, I need full minimax with alpha-beta and move ordering to run fast, but as a safety net I'll add iterative deepening with a time limit plus immediate win/block heuristics, starting by precomputing the 49 winning lines and checking for forced wins first.

If no immediate win exists, I'll block any opponent winning move, favoring blocks that also create my own threat, then fall back to negamax with iterative deepening under a ~0.7s budget, using bitmask representations of lines for fast win-checking limited to lines through the just-played cell. For evaluation I'm scoring lines by counts of mine-vs-theirs (favoring open two-in-a-rows), adding a center-cell bonus, and checking for immediate wins at leaf nodes to weight them heavily.

If the opponent has two or more open winning threats and I have none, I recognize the position as lost since I can only block one line before they complete the other. For the opening move, if the board is empty I'll just take the center since it's the strongest first move, and I'll track whose turn it is by counting pieces already placed. I'm setting up iterative deepening starting at depth 2, keeping the best move found at each completed depth and checking the clock between iterations to stay within the time budget.

Writing move ordering logic...

I'm estimating branching factor and node counts for a 3x3x3 game tree to see how deep alpha-beta pruning can search within budget, likely reaching depth 4-5 early and deeper later as fewer cells remain.

Writing bitboard move generation...

I'm scoring lines based on open threats — counting two-in-a-rows for each side and weighting near-wins heavily, returning large win/loss values when a live threat exists, and handling popcount efficiently for the 3-bit line masks.

Now I'm sketching the negamax search structure with alpha-beta pruning, adding periodic time checks against a deadline so the search can bail out via a timeout exception when it runs too long.

I'm working out win detection and forced-move logic: if I have an immediate winning move I return early with a score favoring faster wins, and if the opponent has one or more threats I need to restrict my move choices to blocking cells or recognize a loss when there are two or more unstoppable threats. I'm also planning to precompute threat cells for both sides by scanning each line mask for the pattern of two of one color and zero of the other.

For the search itself I'm setting a win score constant biased by remaining empty cells so quicker wins score higher, adding a simple transposition table keyed by the (me, opp) bitboards to cache results, and structuring the root search as iterative deepening that stops early on timeout or once a forced win is found. I'm also handling the opening move specially, defaulting to the center cell when the board is empty.

For move ordering I'm using a static priority based on how many lines each cell participates in, favoring the center, then corners, then face centers, then edge centers, while also letting the transposition table's best move take priority at the root. For timing I'm giving the search a conservative half-second budget with periodic time checks every few hundred nodes to stay safely under any real time limit.

Now I'm writing the code to enumerate every winning line across the 3x3x3 grid.

Finishing the line-generation logic, then setting up bitmask constants and a fast popcount for evaluation, followed by negamax search with alpha-beta pruning, a transposition table, and a timeout mechanism to bound root move selection.

For move ordering I'm handling forced blocks: if the opponent has threats, I compute the union of threat cells as a bitmask and check its popcount—if it's a single cell, that's the only legal move to consider, otherwise it's a genuine double threat I can't stop. Finally I convert the chosen bit index back into (i,j,k) coordinates, with a fallback to the first empty cell to guarantee legality.

I'm wrapping the whole search in a try/except so if anything goes wrong, I fall back to a simple heuristic policy: check for an immediate win, then a forced block, then prefer center, then corners, then any empty cell. The policy function converts the board into bitmasks for my pieces and the opponent's, computes the empty mask, and returns the center move on an empty board, otherwise proceeding through the win-check and block-check logic before falling into the full search.

For the actual search, I'm setting a time deadline of about 0.5 seconds from the start to stay safely under the 1-second limit, checking the clock every 256 nodes to avoid overhead. I'm writing a negamax function that increments a node counter, raises a timeout exception if the deadline passes, and detects a draw when no empty cells remain, then scans each winning line to identify masks where I have two-in-a-row with an open third cell (a winning threat) or where the opponent does.

If I have an immediate winning move, I return a large win score adjusted by remaining empty cells; if the opponent has multiple winning threats I return a loss since I can't block them all, otherwise I restrict my move list to just the single blocking cell. When there's no immediate threat, I fall back to move ordering and a heuristic evaluation, computing the position score in the same threat-scanning loop for efficiency, and I'm adding a transposition table keyed on the board bitmasks storing depth, value, flag, and best move for standard alpha-beta lookups.

I'm iterating candidate moves in a fixed priority order, recursing with negamax by flipping perspective and negating the window, and I confirm that since my own winning move was already caught earlier, any move I make in the loop is safe to explore normally — the recursive call handles the opponent's threats from their perspective. I plan to deepen the search iteratively, increasing depth until I hit a time limit or exhaust the empty cells.

I'm ordering cells by how many winning lines pass through them, then writing a root-level search function that mirrors the negamax logic but also tracks and returns the best move, prioritizing the previous iteration's best move first in the loop.
